API_IPC.summary: V2 IPC function table appended after uart1 in the root API. Functions: self(), find(path_or_unique_filename), send(), receive(), pending().
API_IPC.notes: Requires firmware and SDK with Stage 25 IPC. The GUI Designer virtual Messenger component provides code-free sending and cooperative automatic reception.

SIDBOX_IPC_MESSAGE.summary: OS-copied IPC payload: sender instance ID, application-defined type, data length and up to 64 payload bytes.
SIDBOX_IPC_MESSAGE.notes: Payload is raw bytes, NOT necessarily a NUL-terminated C string. Copy at most 64 bytes and add a terminator when displaying text.

SIDBOX_IPC_MAX_DATA.summary: Maximum IPC payload size, currently 64 bytes.

SIDBOX_IPC_QUEUE_DEPTH.summary: Maximum messages waiting in one receiving applet mailbox, currently 8.

SIDBOX_IPC_OK.summary: IPC return code indicating successful send or receive.

SIDBOX_IPC_EMPTY.summary: Receive found no pending message; normal for nonblocking polling.

SIDBOX_IPC_BAD_ARG.summary: Invalid IPC argument, including a payload larger than 64 bytes.

SIDBOX_IPC_NO_CONTEXT.summary: The caller has no valid applet execution context.

SIDBOX_IPC_NO_RECIPIENT.summary: No live receiving applet matches the requested target/instance ID.

SIDBOX_IPC_QUEUE_FULL.summary: Recipient already has eight pending messages; try later.

SIDBOX_IPC_NO_MEMORY.summary: Firmware could not allocate mailbox memory.

API_Root.summary: Root API table at the SIDBOX OS interface. V2 applets use the fixed SRAM API pointer; the SDK provides macro API.
API_Root.notes: Never change member ordering. New tables must be appended to preserve older applet ABI offsets.

guides.title: 01 - Welcome to SIDBOX and CoderGirl
guides.summary: CoderGirl is the computer program used to write software for SIDBOX. SIDBOX is the device that runs the finished programs. A small program running on SIDBOX is called an applet. A GUI applet has windows and controls such as buttons and labels.
guides.notes:
A quick vocabulary guide:
• IDE: the editor used to write, design and build programs.
• SDK: the headers and libraries that let programs use SIDBOX features.
• GUI: graphical user interface — windows, buttons and other controls.
• Gadget: the name used for a GUI control.
• Source code: C instructions written or generated for an applet.
• Build/compile: turn source code into a runnable .app file.
• .sbui: a GUI Designer layout file.
Start with a small V2 GUI applet; no previous SIDBOX programming is required.
guides.example:
/* Common files in a GUI applet project:
   myapp.proj       project settings
   mainwindow.sbui   editable window design
   mainwindow.c      C code generated by Designer
   myapp.app         finished program for SIDBOX
*/

guides.title: 02 - Make a first GUI applet
guides.summary: Create a simple window that says Hello SIDBOX. This exercise uses GUI Designer, so there is no need to write a window procedure from scratch.
guides.notes:
1. In CoderGirl, create a GUI project.
2. Select the relocatable ARM ELF (V2/CGARM) applet format in project settings.
3. Open GUI Designer for the project window.
4. Add a Label gadget to the window. Set its visible text to Hello SIDBOX.
5. Save the .sbui design and generate its C source using Designer.
6. Build the project to create a .app file.
7. Copy that .app to the SIDBOX SD card and launch it.
If the build reports an error, read the first compiler error rather than the last one. Subsequent errors may be consequences of the first.
guides.example:
/* No C needs to be typed for this first exercise.
   GUI Designer creates the window and label code.
   The label's Text property is: Hello SIDBOX
*/

guides.title: 03 - Understand the Designer and generated code
guides.summary: The canvas shows where gadgets will appear. Select a gadget to edit its properties. The Designer saves the layout as .sbui and generates C source when requested.
guides.notes:
A gadget has a C variable name (such as lbl1 or btn1). Code uses that name to refer to the gadget. Designer also generates named callbacks — functions that run when an event happens.
IMPORTANT: Add handwritten code only inside a generated USER block, because code outside those blocks can be replaced when the design is regenerated. Save the .sbui before regenerating source.

guides.title: 04 - Add a label and change its text
guides.summary: A Label shows text on a window. Its C variable lets a button, timer or message callback change that text later.
guides.notes:
1. In Designer, add a Label and give it a name such as lbl1.
2. Set its Text property to Ready.
3. Make the label wide enough for the words you want to display.
4. Generate the C source.
5. To update it from code, use the example inside an appropriate callback USER block.
Why size matters: a 1×1-pixel label can look correct initially but have text disappear during partial screen repainting. Use realistic width and height.
guides.example:
/* Inside a generated callback USER block: */
SBOS_LabelSetText(lbl1, "Hello from SIDBOX!");

guides.title: 05 - Make a button do something
guides.summary: A button runs its Activate callback when clicked. The easiest first button changes a label on the same window.
guides.notes:
1. Add a Label named lbl1 and a Button named btn1 in Designer.
2. Give the Button visible text such as Click Me.
3. Save and generate the C source.
4. Find the generated On_btn1_Activate callback.
5. Put the example in that callback’s USER block.
6. Build and run. Clicking the button should change the label.
The Designer manages the button-event connection; beginners do not need to write a complete window-message dispatcher.
guides.example:
/* Inside On_btn1_Activate(...) USER block: */
SBOS_LabelSetText(lbl1, "You clicked it!");

guides.title: 06 - Learn a little C without being overwhelmed
guides.summary: CoderGirl applets are written in C. A variable stores a value, a function performs work, and an if statement chooses what to do.
guides.notes:
The example declares an integer named count. The = sign assigns a value. count++ adds one. The if statement tests a condition. Text between quotation marks is a string. A semicolon ends most statements.
A callback is an ordinary C function that CoderGirl calls for an event. Small snippets are most useful when placed in a generated USER block; they are not whole applets.
guides.example:
int count = 0;              /* create a number */
count++;                   /* increase by one */
if (count == 1) {          /* compare with 1 */
    dbug("First press");   /* write debug output */
}

guides.title: 07 - Build, launch and fix the first error
guides.summary: Building creates a .app file for SIDBOX. A compiler error means CoderGirl could not finish the build; it does not mean the SIDBOX hardware is broken.
guides.notes:
1. Save the .sbui and generate the C code.
2. Build the project in the IDE using its configured V2 CGARM backend.
3. If the build succeeds, locate the generated .app named in the build output.
4. Copy the .app to the SIDBOX SD card and start it on the device.
5. If the build fails, open the reported filename and line number and fix the FIRST error, then build again.
Common causes: a misspelled gadget variable, a missing semicolon, code pasted outside a function, or an SDK newer/older than the firmware.
guides.example:
/* Two typical compiler errors:

   error: expected ';' before '}'
   -> A statement may be missing a semicolon.

   error: 'lbl1' undeclared
   -> Check the gadget's actual C variable name.

   Compiler errors are build-time messages,
   not messages sent to a running applet.
*/

guides.title: 08 - What is an API?
guides.summary: An API is a set of functions that applets call to ask SIDBOX to perform tasks, such as creating a label or sending a message. The SDK declares which functions are available.
guides.notes:
The simplest way to start is with the SBOS_* convenience names shown in this Cheatsheet. Underneath, many call entries in the API table via the API pointer. Both reach the same SIDBOX services.
The API pointer is not a gadget variable. A C arrow (->) means “access a member through a pointer.”
Use F8 to find an API, read its parameters and copy its example. Do not guess function names.

guides.title: 09 - Run something repeatedly with a timer
guides.summary: A timer requests a callback at intervals. For example, a program might refresh a clock display or check whether a new message has arrived.
guides.notes:
For a GUI project, use the virtual Timer component in Designer where possible. It is not a visible button or label. Configure its interval and put the desired actions in its generated callback.
Timers are cooperative: callbacks should finish quickly rather than pause the applet for a long time. A manually created timer must be cancelled and freed when no longer needed. Designer-generated components manage their own lifecycle.

guides.title: 10 - Add a menu
guides.summary: Menus organise commands such as File, About and Quit. GUI Designer has a Menu Editor for adding titles and their individual items.
guides.notes:
1. Open the Menu Editor for the window.
2. Add a menu title such as File.
3. Add an item such as About.
4. Save/generate the .sbui.
5. Click that item in the Designer preview to navigate to its generated callback.
6. Put the desired action in that callback’s USER block.
Menus do not have to be drawn manually: the SIDBOX GUI renders the menu and handles item selection.

guides.title: 11 - Read a file from the SD card
guides.summary: Applets can read files stored on the SIDBOX SD card. A file slot is a small number used to refer to an open file.
guides.notes:
The example opens slot 0 for reading, attempts to read up to 64 bytes and then closes the slot. Check result codes before using the data.
count tells how many bytes were actually read; it may be smaller than the buffer size. Raw file data is NOT automatically a C string. The example belongs inside a function or callback and requires apis.h. File paths should match actual files on the card.

guides.title: 12 - What is inter-program messaging (IPC)?
guides.summary: IPC means Inter-Process Communication: one running applet sends a small message to another. A Messenger is a virtual gadget, meaning it has no visible control on the window.
guides.notes:
A sender chooses a receiver by applet filename, such as ipc_rx.app. A message has a type (a number chosen by the programmer) and up to 64 bytes of data. Every receiver has a mailbox holding up to 8 messages.
The receiver must be running when the sender tries to find it. If it is closed, sending can fail; this is normal. Messages are copied by SIDBOX, so two applets do not need to share memory pointers. IPC requires the V2 SDK and matching firmware.
guides.example:
/* Two running applets, for example:

   ipc_tx.app  --sends-->  ipc_rx.app

   Message type: 1
   Message text: PING

   Each applet has its own window and memory.
*/

guides.title: 13 - Receive messages using virtual Messenger
guides.summary: GUI Designer can check for incoming messages automatically. Add a Messenger to a receiving applet, enable receiving, and use its generated On Message callback.
guides.notes:
1. Create a V2 GUI project and add a Label called lbl1.
2. In the virtual components area, add a Messenger called messenger1.
3. Set Receive Enabled to Yes (the default polling interval is 25 ms).
4. Save/generate the C code.
5. Find On_messenger1_Message and put the example in its USER block.
6. Build and launch this receiver before starting the sender.
The incoming message includes sender, type, length and data. The data is a byte array, not necessarily a zero-terminated string.

guides.title: 14 - Send a message with NO handwritten IPC code
guides.summary: To make a sending applet, configure a Messenger target and connect a Button to it using Designer properties. The Button will send the configured message when clicked.
guides.notes:
1. Create a second V2 GUI project (the sender).
2. Add a virtual Messenger named messenger1.
3. Set Target applet filename to ipc_rx.app. Turn Receive Enabled off if this sender does not need to receive.
4. Add a Button. Set its visible caption to Send.
5. In the Button properties select IPC Messenger = messenger1.
6. Set IPC message type = 1 and IPC message text = PING.
7. Save/generate/build and run it beside the receiver.
Click Send. The receiver from guide 13 will display “Received 4 bytes”. Do not add a second manual send in the same Button callback or it will send twice.
guides.example:
/* Designer settings, not C to paste:
   Messenger target : ipc_rx.app
   Receive enabled  : No
   Button messenger : messenger1
   Button type      : 1
   Button text      : PING

   Designer generates the send operation.
*/

guides.title: 15 - Send and receive messages directly in C
guides.summary: Programs can also use IPC without the Designer’s automatic send action. This is useful when message content changes while an applet runs.
guides.notes:
This example belongs inside a function in a V2 applet with #include "apis.h". find() returns the current receiver instance ID, or 0 if it cannot find a unique matching applet. send() returns 0 for success; negative values indicate errors.
The receiving applet can process messages using the Messenger callback (guide 13) or the nonblocking API->ipc->receive() call. Never store a receiver ID permanently: closing and reopening the receiver creates a new ID.

guides.title: 16 - Closing an applet safely
guides.summary: Closing an applet releases its windows and owned resources. A newly opened copy of the same applet is a new instance, not a continuation of the previous one.
guides.notes:
If an applet has a Messenger mailbox, unread messages belong to the old instance and must not appear in the new one. Timers created manually should be cancelled and freed. Designer-created virtual timers and Messenger polling are managed by generated lifecycle code.
Avoid keeping pointers to another applet’s memory, and avoid placing very large arrays inside callback functions. Use the documented applet RAM/stack limits when designing bigger programs.

guides.title: 17 - GUI drawing versus graphics drawing
guides.summary: For ordinary windowed programs, add GUI gadgets in Designer. SIDBOX repaints windows and gadgets when parts of the screen change. Graphics-mode programs use a separate drawing setup.
guides.notes:
Windowed GUI applications should not casually replace global LCD or framebuffer settings. Draw into a suitable GUI gadget or follow its supported drawing callback pattern.
The example below is a graphics primitive snippet, not a complete GUI applet. It only makes sense after a graphics-mode project has configured its drawing buffer. For a first program, use Designer labels and buttons instead.

guides.title: 18 - Choosing V1 or V2
guides.summary: CoderGirl can build older V1 applets and newer V2 applets. For a new GUI project that uses Messenger, choose V2 (relocatable ARM ELF / CGARM).
guides.notes:
V1 is the original fixed-address applet format, mainly for existing programs. V2 uses relocatable applets and provides the modern per-applet execution environment.
The IPC functions documented here have been tested with V2 applets. Do not assume a V1 applet can use V2 IPC without separate compatibility support. Many standard GUI concepts apply to either format, but their build and memory models differ.
guides.example:
/* New project needing IPC?
   Project format: V2 / CGARM

   Maintaining an existing old applet?
   Keep its original V1 settings unless deliberately porting it.
*/

guides.title: 01 - V1 games vs V2 GUI applets
guides.summary: Choose the right project type before creating a game.
guides.notes:
A V1 Game project is for games with scrolling levels, a controllable player, sprites, collision, enemies, inventory and quests. A V2 GUI project is for window-based applications such as calculators or file managers.

1. Create a new project and choose the V1 Gaming option.
2. Open Game Designer to build your level visually.
3. Save the design and use Update Game Project to prepare the game for building.

Tip: The Game Engines guides describe V1 games. You do not need to understand the generated C code to start designing a level.
guides.example:
Making a platform game? Choose V1 Gaming.
Making a window with buttons and text fields? Choose V2 GUI.

guides.title: 02 - Explore Game Designer
guides.summary: Find your way around Game Designer and its main editing areas.
guides.notes:
1. Open Game Designer from your V1 Gaming project.
2. Look in Game Resources for Sprites, Game Objects, Sounds, Backgrounds, Tile Atlases and other assets.
3. Select a sprite and place or move it on the world canvas.
4. The visible 480×320 LCD frame shows what the player can see at once. A level can extend far beyond it.
5. Open Tilemap Editor to paint floors and walls. Right-click a placed sprite to configure its behaviour.
6. Save Design when finished.

Tip: Middle-mouse drag moves the editor view. This does not move objects in the game.
guides.example: Try it: Add a sprite, drag it outside the LCD frame, then move the editor view to find it again.

guides.title: 03 - Save, update and build your game
guides.summary: Save a game design, generate its game files and compile it.
guides.notes:
1. Create a V1 Gaming project and open Game Designer.
2. Add a player, some ground and any other objects you want.
3. Choose Save Design to keep your edits.
4. Choose Update Game Project. This checks required resources and creates the files the game uses.
5. Correct any reported errors, then choose Build.
6. Copy any required map, graphics or music files to the TF/SD card before playing on SIDBOX.

Important: When CoderGirl creates main.c and you have not edited it, the IDE can update it for you. Once you edit main.c, the IDE protects your version. If you later need the latest example code, look in maingame.c.txt. Update Game Project makes backups before replacing generated files.

You can build your first game without manually editing C.
guides.example: Game Designer → Save Design → Update Game Project → Build → Run on SIDBOX.

guides.title: 04 - Scrolling worlds and the camera
guides.summary: Understand why a scrolling game’s positions differ from what is on screen.
guides.notes:
A world position describes where something is in the whole level. A screen position describes where it appears within the current camera view.

1. Put a sprite a long way to the right of the starting area.
2. Move the camera view and notice the sprite can appear in different screen positions.
3. The sprite has not moved in the world: only the camera changed.

Game Designer and generated collision code handle this distinction for ordinary game objects. Avoid manually moving objects to compensate for the camera.
guides.example: Example: A coin at world X = 800 appears near the left edge when the camera has scrolled to X = 780.

guides.title: 01 - Advanced Platformer overview
guides.summary: Discover what the Advanced Platformer Game Builder can create.
guides.notes:
Start with a player and a tilemap, then add Game Objects that make the level interactive. You can create springs, doors, switches, enemies, moving platforms, collectables and hazards without writing their basic behaviour in C.

For conversations and inventory, open Adventure Editor. For quests, use Quest Editor. For connections between objects, open Visual Nodes. For additional levels, use World Manager.

A good first project is one small room with a floor, a player, a coin and a door. Save Design and Update Game Project after changing game behaviour.
guides.example: First project idea: Player jumps onto a platform, collects a key, and unlocks a door.

guides.title: 02 - Paint ground, walls and hazards
guides.summary: Paint level graphics and choose which parts the player can stand on.
guides.notes:
Graphics and collision are two separate layers. A tile can look like a wall without being solid, or be solid without visible artwork.

1. Open Tilemap Editor and select a Tile Atlas (the sheet of small graphics).
2. Paint ground and scenery on the graphics layer.
3. Choose a collision brush and paint solid areas where the player must stop.
4. Use slope, hazard or one-way collision types where they fit your level.
5. Save the tilemap, then Update Game Project.

Important: If a Door Game Object must open, do not also paint permanent solid collision across the doorway; the door would disappear but the invisible wall would remain.
guides.example: Try it: Paint a stone floor, add solid collision beneath it, and leave the sky with no collision.

guides.title: 03 - Player movement and jumping
guides.summary: Set up player movement, jumping and collision in a platform game.
guides.notes:
The platformer controller handles gravity, jumping, floors, walls and slopes. The game files generated by Game Designer already connect the normal movement steps.

1. Place and configure a player sprite.
2. Paint a solid floor in Tilemap Editor.
3. Save Design and choose Update Game Project.
4. Build and test left/right movement and jumping.
5. Adjust the Player or Physics Profile if the player moves too quickly, slowly or jumps too high.

You do not need to copy physics functions into main.c for a normal generated project. If you choose to customise the game loop in C later, read the generated maingame.c.txt example and keep its update order.
guides.example: Try it: Change the player's jump strength, rebuild, and compare how high they jump.

guides.title: 04 - Sprites and Game Objects are two views
guides.summary: Learn the difference between a sprite and a Game Object.
guides.notes:
A sprite is a picture placed in the world. A Game Object is that same sprite with an assigned gameplay behaviour, such as a door, coin or spring.

1. Select a placed sprite on the world canvas.
2. Right-click and choose Configure Game Object.
3. Choose a behaviour and save its properties.
4. Look under Game Objects in Game Resources. This is another way to select the configured sprite, not an extra copy.

Tip: Moving the object on the canvas moves the actual placed sprite. You do not need to move two separate items.
guides.example: Example: Place a red gem sprite → Configure Game Object → Collectable. It appears in the Sprites and Game Objects trees.

guides.title: 05 - Hitboxes and activation state
guides.summary: Use hitboxes and starting state to decide when an object can be touched.
guides.notes:
A hitbox is the invisible rectangle used to detect contact with the player. It can be smaller or larger than the visible artwork.

1. Right-click a placed PPB sprite and choose Configure Game Object.
2. Select a behaviour such as Collectable or Door.
3. Adjust Collision width and Collision height until the displayed hitbox fits the object.
4. Leave Active when the level starts enabled for an object that should appear immediately.
5. Turn it off for an item that a switch, key or other action should reveal later.

Tip: Use an appropriately sized sprite at 100% scale for game objects. A disabled object does not behave as an active target.
guides.example: Example: A secret gem starts inactive. A hidden switch uses Enable to make it appear.

guides.title: 06 - Collectables: coins, health, gems and keys
guides.summary: Make items that the player can pick up for points, health or inventory.
guides.notes:
1. Place a PPB sprite in the world and configure it as Collectable.
2. Choose Coin, Health, Gem, Key or Custom and set its value.
3. Decide what happens on pickup. For a direct Health change, turn Show in Inventory OFF and choose Player Health as the target.
4. For a carried item, turn Show in Inventory ON and set up its Inventory definition in Adventure Editor.
5. Set an optional pickup sound or respawn delay, then Save Design and Update Game Project.

A collectable can start hidden and appear after a trigger or defeated enemy. Quest keys and unique rewards should not be added to repeatable random enemy loot.
guides.example: Try it: Place a Health pickup → Show in Inventory OFF → Apply to Player Health → test the HUD.

guides.title: 07 - Walkthrough: key unlocks a door
guides.summary: Build a simple puzzle in which picking up a key opens a door.
guides.notes:
1. Place a door sprite, choose Configure Game Object, and set Door / Solid blocker.
2. Leave the door active when the level starts and size its collision rectangle.
3. Place a key sprite and set it to Collectable → Key.
4. In the key properties, select the placed door as the target and choose Disable target.
5. Set the key's respawn delay to 0 for a single-use key.
6. Save Design, Update Game Project and test collecting the key.

Important: Leave the doorway free from permanent solid tilemap collision so it becomes passable after the door turns off.
guides.example: Door starts ON. Key pickup → Disable door. Player can now walk through.

guides.title: 08 - Doors and solid blockers
guides.summary: Create a barrier that can open, close or appear during the game.
guides.notes:
1. Place a door or barrier sprite and configure it as Door / Solid blocker.
2. Size the hitbox to cover the doorway.
3. Choose whether it starts active (blocking) or inactive (open).
4. Make a key, switch or Visual Nodes action target that door.
5. Use Disable to open it, Enable to close it, or Toggle to swap between the two.

A Door / Solid blocker uses solid collision when active. A moving lift is different: players normally land on it from above. Do not put permanent solid tiles through an opening door.
guides.example:
Hidden barrier: Active at start OFF + Switch ENABLE.
Normal locked door: Active at start ON + Key DISABLE.

guides.title: 09 - Switches: touch or FIRE2
guides.summary: Make a switch activate by touch or by pressing FIRE2.
guides.notes:
1. Place a switch sprite and configure it as Trigger / Switch.
2. Set a hitbox that the player can reach.
3. Choose the Game Object that the switch controls and select Enable, Disable or Toggle.
4. Leave Require FIRE2 while touching OFF for a pressure plate. Turn it ON for a switch the player must press.
5. Leave Remove switch after activation OFF if the switch should be usable again.
6. Save Design and Update Game Project.

FIRE2 is the interaction button, separate from the normal jump button. A repeatable switch waits for another activation rather than switching on every game frame.
guides.example:
Pressure plate: FIRE2 OFF → toggles a door on touch.
Wall switch: FIRE2 ON → toggles when the player presses FIRE2 nearby.

guides.title: 10 - One-shot triggers and room discovery
guides.summary: Make a trigger run once for a secret or special event.
guides.notes:
1. Place a sprite in the level and configure it as Trigger / Switch.
2. Pick a target and an action, such as Disable a door or Enable a hidden gem.
3. Enable Remove switch after activation.
4. Choose touch activation or Require FIRE2.
5. Save the design, update the game and walk into the trigger.

After its first activation the trigger stops working during that run. If progress must survive restarting SIDBOX, use the game's Save Points and save slots.
guides.example: Secret passage: Trigger activates once → Disable hidden barrier → player enters new room.

guides.title: 11 - Springers: normal bounce
guides.summary: Bounce the player upward with a Spring / Bouncer.
guides.notes:
1. Place a spring sprite and choose Configure Game Object → Spring / Bouncer.
2. Adjust the hitbox to cover the top of the spring.
3. Set Spring upward launch. Start with a modest value and increase it after testing.
4. Keep Spring sideways launch at 0 for a straight-up bounce.
5. Save the design, update the project and test landing on the spring.

By default, the spring activates when the player lands on top. Combining a fresh jump press with a spring boost is an optional setting, not the default.
guides.example: Try it: Put a spring beneath a high ledge and adjust its upward launch until the player can reach it.

guides.title: 12 - Springers: touch and directional launches
guides.summary: Make springs that bounce from the side, ceiling or any direction.
guides.notes:
1. Create a Spring / Bouncer as in the previous guide.
2. Enable Activate on touch (any side).
3. Set Spring sideways launch to a negative number for left or positive for right.
4. Keep an upward value if you also want a rising bounce.
5. Test contact from different directions and adjust the hitbox.

A touch spring activates when the player enters its area; the player must leave it before it can trigger again. Large launch values can make movement difficult to control.
guides.example: Example: Put a spring on the right wall and use a negative sideways launch to bounce the player left.

guides.title: 13 - Springers: slidy inertia and jump boost
guides.summary: Give a spring a sliding launch or optional jump boost.
guides.notes:
1. Configure a Spring / Bouncer and set an upward and sideways launch.
2. Enable Slidy kickback when you want the sideways push to carry on after leaving the spring.
3. Test it on different Player Physics Profiles. Ice stays slippery longer; Water slows movement more quickly.
4. If you want a fresh jump press to add extra height, enable Combine jump + spring launch separately.
5. Save, update and test the results on the game device.

For games with a manually edited main.c, these advanced spring settings may need the extra physics binding shown in the generated maingame.c.txt. A normal IDE-generated starter already provides the standard integration.
guides.example: Try it: Launch the player across a gap using a spring with Slidy ON, then compare Slidy OFF.

guides.title: 14 - Moving lifts and platforms
guides.summary: Carry the player on a moving platform or lift.
guides.notes:
1. Place a platform sprite and configure it as Moving platform / Lift.
2. Adjust its collision width and height to match the surface the player stands on.
3. To make it move, create a Spline path with at least two points.
4. Select that path in the lift's Movement spline setting.
5. Save Design, Update Game Project and test standing on the platform as it travels.

Lifts act like surfaces the player can land on from above. They are not solid walls on every side. Test the path near walls to make sure the player cannot become trapped.
guides.example: Example: Draw a vertical path between the ground floor and a ledge, then assign it to a lift.

guides.title: 15 - Conveyors
guides.summary: Move the player sideways while they stand on a conveyor belt.
guides.notes:
1. Place a conveyor sprite on the level.
2. Configure it as Conveyor and size the surface hitbox.
3. Set Conveyor px/frame to a positive value for right or a negative value for left.
4. Save Design and Update Game Project.
5. Test walking, jumping and stopping on the belt.

You can optionally attach the conveyor to a spline to make the whole platform travel. A conveyor is a surface, not a full solid wall.
guides.example:
Conveyor px/frame = +2 → moves the player right.
Conveyor px/frame = -2 → moves the player left.

guides.title: 16 - Splines: move objects through a level
guides.summary: Draw a path and make a Game Object follow it.
guides.notes:
A Spline is a path made of points. It is useful for moving lifts, travelling platforms and other moving objects.

1. In Game Designer, add a Spline and place at least two path points.
2. Give the path a recognisable name.
3. Place a sprite, configure it as a compatible moving Game Object, then open its Movement spline setting.
4. Choose your path from the list.
5. Save Design and Update Game Project.

The generated starter code runs attached moving objects for you. Do not add a second manual movement update for the same object.
guides.example: Try it: Create a three-point path that rises, crosses a gap and returns; assign it to a Moving Lift.

guides.title: 17 - Sprite animation on objects
guides.summary: Animate a Game Object using several frames of sprite artwork.
guides.notes:
1. Prepare a PPB sprite sheet containing the animation frames.
2. Open the object's Game Object Properties.
3. Turn on Animate sprite frames.
4. Choose the first frame, number of frames and Frames per picture (how long each frame stays visible).
5. Choose Loop, Ping-pong or Once and test it in the running game.

The animation changes the picture, not the object's gameplay behaviour. A moving platform can animate while it moves.
guides.example: First frame 0, Number of frames 4, Frames per picture 5, Mode Loop → a simple four-frame animation.

guides.title: 18 - Tile atlas animation
guides.summary: Animate water, lights or other tiles directly in the Tile Atlas.
guides.notes:
Animated tiles are useful when many map cells should share the same moving graphic, such as a river.

1. Open Tilemap Editor and select the Tile Atlas.
2. Set up the graphic frames for the tile animation.
3. Paint the animated tile wherever it is needed.
4. Save the tilemap and Update Game Project.
5. Make sure the latest matching PPB artwork is on the TF/SD card when using external artwork.

You do not need to create a separate Game Object for every animated map tile.
guides.example: Try it: Set up two or more water frames, then paint the same animated tile across a river.

guides.title: 19 - Sound effects, radius and channels
guides.summary: Play sounds when the player picks up an item or uses an object.
guides.notes:
1. Add a suitable WAV under Game Resources → Sounds.
2. Configure the Game Object that should make the sound.
3. Find its Sound / Audio settings and choose the desired event sound, such as pickup or spring launch.
4. If available, adjust its audio channel, distance or fade settings.
5. Save Design, Update Game Project and test with SIDBOX audio enabled.

Tip: Sounds using the same channel can interrupt each other. Pick different channels for sounds that need to overlap.
guides.example: Example: Assign a short chime to a Gem Collectable's pickup event.

guides.title: 20 - Fix common game problems
guides.summary: Check the most common causes of an object not working.
guides.notes:
Try these checks in order:
1. Save Design, then choose Update Game Project and rebuild.
2. Check that the sprite uses a valid PPB resource and is configured as the intended Game Object.
3. Make sure its hitbox is large enough for the player to touch.
4. Check its Active when the level starts setting and any required FIRE2 interaction.
5. If a switch or key controls something, confirm the selected target and action.
6. For opening doors, remove any permanent solid collision covering the doorway.
7. For missing artwork or audio, confirm the required files are on the TF/SD card.
8. If Update Game Project reports an error, use Go to Problem to open the relevant editor and correct it.

Avoid manually modifying generated game helper files. Change the design and regenerate instead. If you have modified main.c, compare it with the updated maingame.c.txt instructions.
guides.example: Door does not open? Check: Door starts active → Key targets that Door → Action is Disable → no solid tile inside doorway.

guides.title: 21 - Puzzle recipes to try
guides.summary: Try small puzzles by combining Game Objects already in the editor.
guides.notes:
Start with one idea at a time:
1. Secret door: a one-time trigger disables a hidden barrier.
2. Repeatable switch: FIRE2 toggles a door open and closed.
3. Treasure room: a trigger enables a gem that started hidden.
4. Lift puzzle: a moving platform carries the player to a key.
5. Spring challenge: a sideways spring sends the player across a gap.

To save puzzle progress between sessions, configure the normal Save Point and Save/Load features. An unsaved game session should not be expected to survive restarting SIDBOX.
guides.example: Beginner challenge: Make a pressure plate reveal a gem. Then add a second switch that closes the entrance.

guides.title: 22 - Switches that start or stop music
guides.summary: Start or stop background music with a switch.
guides.notes:
1. Import a suitable music file under Game Resources → Music.
2. Place and configure a Trigger / Switch.
3. Find the switch's music settings and choose Play selected tune, then pick a Music resource.
4. Alternatively, choose Stop current music to stop whatever is playing.
5. Choose whether the switch activates by touch or FIRE2.
6. Save Design, Update Game Project and ensure any external music files are on the TF/SD card.

Playing a new track replaces the currently playing music. You can use the same switch to control another object too.
guides.example: Example: Walking into a boss room activates a one-shot switch that starts the boss music.

guides.title: 23 - Export embedded C or SD .map tilemaps
guides.summary: Choose whether a world’s tilemap is built into the game or loaded from the card.
guides.notes:
Tilemaps have two storage choices:
• Embedded: The map is included when the game is built. Repeating data may be compressed automatically to save space.
• External .map: The map is a separate file read from the TF/SD card when its world loads.

1. Open Tilemap Editor and choose the required export mode.
2. Save the level and choose Update Game Project.
3. For an external map, copy the generated .map and required PPB artwork to the correct card paths.
4. Build and test entering the world, leaving it, then returning.

Both modes can be used in multi-world games. Collectables, quests and object state are part of the world/game systems, not stored inside the .map tile-data file.
guides.example:
Small self-contained game → Embedded map.
Many large maps on a card → External .map files can be convenient.

guides.title: 24 - Hazard tiles: entering and leaving
guides.summary: Learn when the player enters, stays inside or leaves a hazardous tile.
guides.notes:
A Hazard tile detects contact without acting like a solid wall. It can be used for spikes, hot surfaces or dangerous water.

1. In Tilemap Editor, paint Hazard collision on the tiles that should be dangerous.
2. Save and update the game.
3. Test walking into, standing inside and leaving the area.

There are three contact events: Entered (first touch), Inside (while touching) and Exited (after leaving). Hazards do not automatically decide how much damage to cause. A custom C callback can react to these events; see the generated game example if you want to program your own effects.

Important: Inside can fire on every game frame (about 50 times per second). Do not subtract a whole health point on every call unless that is intentional. For beginner-friendly configurable damage, consider a placed Hazard Zone Game Object.
guides.example: Example: Paint a lava floor with Hazard collision. A custom callback could subtract Health once per second while the player remains inside.

guides.title: 25 - Hazard Zones: dangerous areas
guides.summary: Place a hazard area that detects the player without blocking movement.
guides.notes:
1. Place a sprite or marked area in Game Designer.
2. Configure it as a Hazard Zone Game Object.
3. Resize the hitbox to cover the dangerous area.
4. Choose any available player damage or stat settings in the object's properties.
5. Save Design, Update Game Project and test entering and leaving the zone.

A Hazard Zone can report Entered, Inside and Exited contact. It is not automatically a solid obstacle, and a custom C callback may be used for specialised effects. If the zone remains dangerous while the player stands still, make sure repeated damage is limited to the intended rate.
guides.example: Try it: Put a narrow hazard over a glowing floor tile and check that the player can leave the area.

guides.title: 26 - Stamp Bank: Reusable tile arrangements
guides.summary: Save groups of tiles as reusable stamps for faster map painting.
guides.notes:
A Tile Stamp is a reusable arrangement of graphics and optional collision cells, such as a doorway or a 4×4 patch of stonework.

1. Open Tilemap Editor and find the Stamp Bank on the right.
2. Choose Add, give the stamp a name and set its width and height in tile cells.
3. Select a tile from the atlas and paint into the Stamp Editor grid.
4. Select the finished stamp's thumbnail to use it as the brush.
5. Left-click or drag on the map to place copies; right-click to erase placements.
6. Choose Save to keep editing, or Apply to Design to finish.

Tile Stamps are shared by atlas, so check where a shared stamp is used before changing or deleting it. Placed artwork is exported as ordinary tiles: the game does not need the Stamp Bank at runtime.
guides.example: Try it: Make a 3×2 doorway stamp, paint one doorway, then use the same stamp in another room.

guides.title: 05 - Make your first playable V1 game
guides.summary: Build and play your first V1 platform game without starting from C code.
guides.notes:
1. Create a V1 Gaming project and open Game Designer.
2. Add a player PPB sprite and choose its Player/Physics settings.
3. Open Tilemap Editor, select a Tile Atlas, paint visible ground and add solid collision.
4. Return to Game Designer, place one Collectable and save the design.
5. Choose Update Game Project. Resolve any listed missing-resource problems.
6. Choose Build. Copy required external PPB or .map resources to the TF/SD card and run the game.
7. Try walking, jumping and collecting your item.

CoderGirl can maintain the generated main.c until you edit it yourself. If you do edit it later, your changes are protected and the latest generated example can still be found in maingame.c.txt.
guides.example: First-game checklist: player visible ✓ floor solid ✓ player moves ✓ item collects ✓ game builds ✓

guides.title: 27 - Flip X/Y for individual tile cells
guides.summary: Flip a tile horizontally or vertically without making another picture.
guides.notes:
1. Open Tilemap Editor and select a tile from the atlas.
2. Turn on Cell Flip X to mirror left/right or Cell Flip Y to mirror top/bottom.
3. Click the map to place the flipped tile. The preview shows the result before painting.
4. To flip an existing graphic without replacing it, select Don't change graphic and apply only the flip flags.
5. Save and Update Game Project.

Tile artwork and collision are separate. Flipping a picture does not automatically make its slope collision face the other way.
guides.example: Try it: Paint one arrow tile, then paint its mirror with Cell Flip X.

guides.title: 28 - Mirror stamps while keeping per-cell flips
guides.summary: Mirror an entire Tile Stamp while keeping individual tile flips.
guides.notes:
1. Select a saved stamp in the Tilemap Editor's Stamp Bank.
2. If needed, give individual stamp cells their own Cell Flip X or Y settings.
3. Enable Mirror stamp X or Mirror stamp Y before placing the stamp.
4. Look at the preview and click the map to place the mirrored version.
5. Turn mirroring off to place the original orientation again.

Mirroring changes the newly placed copy, not the saved source stamp. A mirrored graphic stamp can change the direction of ordinary slope collision, so test slope edges after painting.
guides.example: Example: Make one corner decoration stamp, then use Mirror stamp X to decorate the opposite corner.

guides.title: 29 - Save while editing and drag stamps on a stamp-sized grid
guides.summary: Save the map without closing the editor and paint repeating stamps.
guides.notes:
1. In Tilemap Editor, select a Tile Stamp from the Stamp Bank.
2. Press and hold the left mouse button on the map and drag. The brush repeats the stamp on a grid based on that stamp's size.
3. Right-drag to erase whole stamp-sized areas.
4. Press Ctrl+Z to undo a dragged paint operation if the result is wrong.
5. Choose Save to write the design while keeping Tilemap Editor open. Choose Apply to Design when you want to return to Game Designer.

When Save asks about exporting, Yes also writes the level output; No saves the design only. Cancel cannot undo work that was already saved successfully.
guides.example: Try it: Make a 4×2 stone platform stamp, drag across the map, choose Save, and continue painting.

guides.title: 30 - Live tile and stamp placement preview
guides.summary: Preview exactly where the next tile or stamp will be painted.
guides.notes:
1. Select an atlas tile or a saved Tile Stamp.
2. Move the pointer across the map without clicking.
3. A faint preview shows its size, position and any X/Y mirroring.
4. Left-click to paint; drag a stamp to repeat it on its temporary grid.
5. Use right-drag to preview and erase a stamp-sized area.

The preview itself does not change the map. Nothing is placed until you click or drag with the paint tool.
guides.example: Try it: Select a large stamp and move it near the map edge to see its full footprint before placing it.

guides.title: 31 - Make walkable slopes with Collision Stamps
guides.summary: Draw reusable walkable slopes using the Collision Stamp editor.
guides.notes:
A Collision Stamp defines the ground surface with a line made from movable points. It is useful for hills and ramps.

1. Open Tilemap Editor → Collision Stamps and choose Add.
2. Adjust the left and right endpoints and click to insert extra points along the slope.
3. Drag points to shape the ramp; remove an unwanted middle point with right-click.
4. Select the finished slope stamp and paint it on the map.
5. Edit the original stamp later to update all of its placed copies.
6. Save the design and Update Game Project.

Tip: Shift+left-click a placed slope to reopen its shared shape. Add its decorative artwork separately; a collision stamp is not a picture. Apply collision stamps after ordinary graphics stamps if those also paint collision.
guides.example: Try it: Draw a gentle hill with three points, place two copies and then move the middle point.

guides.title: 32 - Edit or erase shared Collision Stamps
guides.summary: Understand how shared Collision Stamps behave when edited or erased.
guides.notes:
A placed Collision Stamp refers back to its original shape. That means changing the shape can update every copy already used in the map.

1. Select a Collision Stamp and place a few copies.
2. Shift+left-click one of its placements to edit the source shape.
3. Move a point and watch the other copies update.
4. Right-drag across a placement to remove the whole collision shape, not only one tile.
5. Save the map, update the project and replace an external .map file on the card if your world uses one.

For old maps with hand-painted slopes, repainting with the newer Collision Stamps may reduce the stored collision data. Keep ordinary tile graphics separate from the slope collision shapes.
guides.example: Example: One hillside stamp used five times can be adjusted once to change all five hills.

guides.title: 33 - Tilemap editor view and brush memory
guides.summary: Reuse Tilemap Editor brush settings and quickly fill connected areas.
guides.notes:
Tilemap Editor remembers useful settings, including the selected brush, zoom and map view, when you reopen it.

1. Choose a normal tile from the Tile Atlas.
2. Click the paint bucket button or press F to turn on Flood Fill.
3. Left-click a connected area to replace its matching tiles; right-click to erase the matching area.
4. Press F again to return to normal painting.
5. Use Ctrl+Z to undo the entire fill, or Ctrl+Y to redo it.

Fill spreads up, down, left and right, not diagonally. If the result is too wide, undo it and check whether the area is separated by a different tile. Selecting a stamp returns to its normal placement tool.
guides.example: Try it: Draw a closed rectangle with one tile type, then Flood Fill its inside with a different tile.

guides.title: 34 - Draw tiles in front of the player
guides.summary: Make foreground scenery that appears in front of the player.
guides.notes:
Foreground tiles are useful for bushes, arches, tall grass or tree branches that the player can walk behind.

1. Open Tilemap Editor and select the artwork you want.
2. Turn on Apply tile flags and Draw in front of player.
3. Paint the foreground graphics where they belong.
4. Save the map and Update Game Project.
5. Run the game and walk behind the artwork to check the layering.

Collision is a separate choice: a foreground tile can be walk-through scenery or a solid obstacle. For stamps, the Draw Front setting can apply to the whole placed stamp or keep each cell's saved value.
guides.example: Try it: Paint tall grass in the foreground so the player's feet disappear behind it while walking.

guides.title: 35 - Copy and paste a tilemap region
guides.summary: Copy part of a map and paste it elsewhere without saving a permanent stamp.
guides.notes:
1. In Tilemap Editor, hold Shift and left-drag a rectangle around the tiles to copy.
2. Move the pointer to preview the copied area at a new location.
3. Left-click to paste. Repeat if you need another copy.
4. Press Escape to leave temporary paste mode.
5. Use Ctrl+Z if a pasted region was placed incorrectly.

A copied region includes its ordinary graphics, collision and tile flags. Collision Stamp shapes are kept together so you do not accidentally copy half a linked slope. The copied brush is temporary and will not be added to the Stamp Bank.
guides.example: Try it: Shift-drag a decorated 4×2 platform, paste it across a gap, then press Escape.

guides.title: 36 - Make custom water, ice or other zones
guides.summary: Create special floor regions such as water, ice or zero gravity.
guides.notes:
Custom collision zones are named map areas that a game can detect. They can be walk-through regions or solid barriers.

1. Open Tilemap Editor and choose a Custom collision type (Custom 1–8).
2. Use Name Zone to give it a helpful name, such as Water.
3. Choose whether Custom is solid should be ON (blocks the player) or OFF (allows walking through).
4. Paint the zone on the collision layer, save and Update Game Project.
5. Test that the player can enter or touch the area as expected.

Advanced option: Custom zones can send Entered, Inside and Exited events to a C callback. To make Water actually change swimming physics, follow the optional generated on_custom_zone example in maingame.c.txt. Simply painting a named zone does not automatically change movement.
guides.example: Try it: Paint Custom 1, name it Water, leave it non-solid. Add swimming behaviour later using the generated example.

guides.title: 37 - Add wind or floating forces (optional C)
guides.summary: Learn what extra movement forces are and when you might use them.
guides.notes:
Forces are optional pushes added to player movement. They can create wind, explosions or floating in space, but this is an advanced C-customisation feature.

Start with normal Player Physics Profiles first. When you are ready to customise C:
1. Open the current generated maingame.c.txt example.
2. Find the optional movement or thruster example.
3. Apply a force before the normal player physics update.
4. Rebuild and test a small force first.

A force applied once gives a push; one applied every frame acts continuously. Negative X pushes left and negative Y pushes up. Do not run two different player physics update functions in the same frame.

guides.title: 38 - Add a Tile Atlas to Game Resources
guides.summary: Register a Tile Atlas without placing it as a visible sprite.
guides.notes:
A Tile Atlas is the sheet of small graphics used to paint a tilemap. It does not have to appear as a large picture on the world canvas.

1. In Game Designer, right-click Game Resources and choose Add Tile Atlas.
2. Select a PPB file containing your tiles.
3. Open Tilemap Editor and select that atlas from the Tile Atlas list.
4. Paint the map, save it and Update Game Project.

If an old project uses a decorative sprite solely to hold the map atlas, its context menu may offer Move to Tile Atlases. Only use this for an atlas-holder sprite, not a visible character or other game sprite.
guides.example: Game Resources → Add Tile Atlas → select terrain.ppb → Tilemap Editor → choose terrain.

guides.title: 39 - Convert PNG pictures into PPB graphics
guides.summary: Convert PNG artwork into SIDBOX PPB graphics using a shared palette.
guides.notes:
SIDBOX graphics use a limited set of palette colours. The PNG converter helps you choose which colours each new image can use.

1. In Game Resources, choose Convert PNG → PPB.
2. Choose whether the new graphic belongs to Sprites, Tile Atlases or Backgrounds.
3. Pick a palette and a colour index range for the image. Index 0 is reserved for transparency.
4. Compare Before and After previews. Try a dithering setting if the image has more colours than the chosen range.
5. Save the new PPB and any required palette file.
6. Import the next image using a different range if the existing colour entries must stay unchanged.

Important: Reusing palette indexes can change colours in artwork already using those indexes. Back up existing .pal and .ppb files before overwriting them; Undo does not restore overwritten image files.
guides.example: Beginner example: Use colours 1–15 for a player sprite and 16–31 for scenery, keeping the same foreground palette.

guides.title: 40 - Keep your main.c edits safe
guides.summary: Learn how CoderGirl protects a main.c file you have edited.
guides.notes:
For a new V1 game, CoderGirl can create and maintain the starter main.c for you.

1. Build your game in Game Designer and use Update Game Project.
2. Leave main.c unedited if you want future updates to keep it in step with the design.
3. If you choose to edit and save main.c yourself, CoderGirl switches it to user-owned and stops replacing it.
4. You can still open maingame.c.txt to see the newest generated starter and copy any changes you need manually.

An older or externally edited main.c is also protected from automatic replacement. Before updates, CoderGirl makes backups. Do not change ownership headers in an attempt to force replacement: the IDE also checks whether the actual file matches its recorded original.
guides.example: Beginner rule: Do not edit main.c unless you mean to maintain it yourself. Game Designer can generate the ordinary game loop.

guides.title: 41 - Make curved hills and loop tracks
guides.summary: Create curved hills and optional loop-the-loop tracks.
guides.notes:
A Bezier Curve helps you turn a straight Collision Stamp into a smooth hill or ramp.

1. Open Tilemap Editor → Collision Stamps and select a slope.
2. Choose Generate Bezier Curve.
3. Move the handles until the preview looks right, then apply it.
4. Place the shape and test how the player walks along it.

For a circular loop, use the separate Loop Tracks tab. Add a loop, set its centre, radius and minimum entry speed, then draw artwork to match it. A loop is a movement track, not an automatically drawn circle or an ordinary solid slope. The player needs enough speed to stay attached while travelling around it. Test in-game before building an entire level around a loop.
guides.example: Try it: Make a shallow curved ramp first. Then create a loop with a straight approach so the player can build speed.

guides.title: 01 - Adventure Editor: NPC conversations
guides.summary: Make a character talk to the player using the Adventure Editor.
guides.notes:
An NPC is a character the player can talk to. Dialogue is the conversation that appears on screen.

1. Place the character's sprite in Game Designer and configure it as an NPC.
2. Open Adventure Editor for that world.
3. Add a Dialogue entry and write what the character says.
4. Select the NPC and assign the dialogue that should start when the player talks to them.
5. Add more dialogue entries and link them if you want a longer conversation.
6. Save the world, choose Update Game Project and talk to the character in the game.

Tip: Dialogue folders help keep large stories organised. Use double-click to open an existing dialogue for editing.
guides.example: Try it: Make a forest guard say “The bridge is closed.” when the player talks to them.

guides.title: 02 - NPC Idle and Talking animations
guides.summary: Give an NPC different animations when waiting and talking.
guides.notes:
1. Prepare the NPC's PPB sprite frames.
2. Open Adventure Editor and select the NPC.
3. Open its Animation Designer.
4. Choose the Idle frames to show when the NPC is not speaking.
5. Choose the Talking frames to play while dialogue is on screen.
6. Set the frame timing, save the world and Update Game Project.

Idle and Talking animations are stored as part of the NPC's Adventure setup. You do not need to create an extra animation sidecar file for these two sequences. Check that the chosen frames exist in the sprite artwork.
guides.example: Example: Idle uses a blinking animation; Talking uses a two-frame mouth movement.

guides.title: 03 - Dialogue choices, wrong items and repeats
guides.summary: Offer dialogue choices and respond to the right or wrong inventory item.
guides.notes:
1. Open Adventure Editor and create the NPC's opening dialogue.
2. Add a Choice if the player should select a reply.
3. If the NPC expects an item, choose the required Inventory Item in the exchange settings.
4. Create follow-up dialogue for receiving the correct item, having no item or offering the wrong item.
5. Use the repeat settings if you want different responses when a player keeps offering unsuitable items.
6. Save, update and test each possible outcome.

Keep item requirements and conversations in Adventure Editor. Visual Nodes can connect dialogue with other game actions, but the dialogue text and item exchange rules are edited here.
guides.example: Example: Guard asks for a pass. Correct pass → “You may enter.” Wrong item → “That is not a pass!”

guides.title: 04 - Inventory, item icons and dropping
guides.summary: Create inventory items the player can carry, use or drop.
guides.notes:
1. Open Adventure Editor → Inventory Items and add a named item.
2. Choose its small icon from registered PPB graphics. Icons may use a single tile or a 2×2 stamp.
3. Place a Collectable sprite in Game Designer.
4. In its properties, turn on Show in Inventory and connect the correct item definition.
5. Choose which actions are allowed, such as Use, Drop or Destroy.
6. Save Design, Update Game Project and collect the item in-game.

Items needed by quests or NPCs may be protected from destruction. If a pickup should change Health instead of entering the bag, turn Show in Inventory OFF and choose a direct player-stat target. Opening Inventory pauses active gameplay until it closes.
guides.example: Try it: Create a “Small Key” with an icon, collect it, open Inventory and check that it appears.

guides.title: 05 - Quests and Journal objectives
guides.summary: Give the player a quest with objectives shown in the Journal.
guides.notes:
A Quest is a goal made from smaller objectives, such as finding an item or activating switches.

1. Open Quest Editor and add a quest with a name and description.
2. Add one or more objectives.
3. For an objective completed by game logic, choose Event signal.
4. Open Visual Nodes and connect a matching Game Object event to that quest objective.
5. Choose Allow objectives in ANY ORDER if players should be able to complete them in any sequence.
6. Save the world, Update Game Project and check the Quest Journal in-game.

All required objectives must be completed, even when their order is flexible. The Journal can show active, tracked and completed quests. Opening it pauses gameplay.
guides.example: Try it: Quest “Open the gate” → activate two switches → show the completed quest in the Journal.

guides.title: 06 - Dialogue thought bubbles and queued speech
guides.summary: Show the player’s thoughts and display several conversations in order.
guides.notes:
The Adventure Editor can show Player Speech as an ordinary line of dialogue or a thought bubble above the player.

1. Open a Player Speech entry in Adventure Editor.
2. Choose Use as thought bubble if that is the effect you want.
3. Choose whether the bubble belongs with this dialogue or the next dialogue, where that option is available.
4. Save and Update Game Project.
5. Test the scene to check the bubble appears at the right moment.

If two events request dialogue almost simultaneously, the game queues the conversations instead of replacing the first one. The second speech may appear after the first finishes.
guides.example: Example: NPC says “Did you hear that?” and the player’s thought bubble shows “I should investigate.”

guides.title: 01 - Events and states: understand the wire colours
guides.summary: Learn the two basic connection types in Visual Nodes: events and states.
guides.notes:
Visual Nodes is a visual way to connect Game Objects, dialogue, quests and game logic.

An EVENT means something happened once, such as “switch activated” or “coin picked up”. Event connections are shown in gold.
A STATE means something is currently true or false, such as “switch is ON”. State connections are shown in teal.

1. Open Visual Nodes for the current world.
2. Find a Trigger / Switch object.
3. Drag from its ON ACTIVATE event to an action when you want an immediate response.
4. Use its ON/OFF state when a logic condition needs to know whether the switch remains on.
5. Save Graph + World after changes.

Tip: Read the socket tooltips if unsure which connection to use. You do not need to edit the game's generated files to create a normal node connection.
guides.example:
Event example: Switch ON ACTIVATE → show dialogue.
State example: Switch ON → AND with another switch's ON state.

guides.title: 02 - AND, OR and NOT: combine switch conditions
guides.summary: Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT logic nodes.
guides.notes:
Logic nodes help you create puzzles involving several switches or other conditions.

AND is true only when all connected conditions are true.
OR is true when at least one connected condition is true.
NOT reverses one condition: ON becomes OFF, or true becomes false.

1. Open Visual Nodes and add the logic node you need.
2. Connect compatible teal STATE outputs from your switches or other objects.
3. Connect the logic result to an action or object state.
4. Save Graph + World and test each combination in the game.

Tip: Start with two switches and one AND node before making a large puzzle. Some nodes add extra inputs as you connect more sources.
guides.example: Two-switch gate: Switch A ON + Switch B ON → AND → make a hidden doorway visible.

guides.title: 03 - COUNTER: count hits, pickups and switches
guides.summary: Count repeated events and respond when the target number is reached.
guides.notes:
A COUNTER is useful when the player must do something several times, such as hit an enemy three times or activate three switches.

1. In Visual Nodes, add a COUNTER logic node and select its placed Game Object owner when asked.
2. Set Target events to the number required.
3. Connect a gold event such as ON ACTIVATE, ON HIT or ON PICKUP to a count input.
4. Use the YES / RESULT state when the count has reached the target.
5. Use NO when the count is still below the target.
6. Connect RESET to a suitable gold event if you want to clear the count and start again.

Each event counts, even if the same source sends several events. YES and NO describe the current counter state; they are not separate pickup or hit events. Save Graph + World and test the required number of actions.
guides.example: Example: Enemy ON HIT → COUNTER (Target = 3) → YES → unlock a door after the third hit.

guides.title: 04 - TIMER: make something happen after a delay
guides.summary: Start a countdown and trigger actions when it starts or finishes.
guides.notes:
A TIMER counts game frames. At 50 frames per second, 250 frames is about five seconds.

1. Add a TIMER node in Visual Nodes and choose the Game Object that owns it.
2. Enter the duration in frames.
3. Connect a gold event to START to begin a fresh countdown.
4. Connect a destination action to FALSE / RUNNING if it should run once when the timer starts or continues.
5. Connect another action to TRUE / FINISHED if it should happen when the time runs out.
6. Use STOP to pause, CONTINUE to resume or RESET to clear the timer.

The RUNNING and FINISHED action outputs are not events that happen every frame. A finished timer can be started again. To make an item appear only once ever, also use a saved pickup counter or quest condition.
guides.example: Timed door: Switch ON ACTIVATE → TIMER START (250 frames); TIMER RUNNING → open door; TIMER FINISHED → close door.

guides.title: 05 - Connect a game event to a quest objective
guides.summary: Complete a quest objective from a switch, collectable or logic result.
guides.notes:
1. In Quest Editor, create a quest and an objective.
2. Choose Event signal as the objective type.
3. Open Visual Nodes. The objective appears as a quest node that can receive an event.
4. Connect a compatible gold event, such as a Trigger's ON ACTIVATE, to that quest objective.
5. Save Graph + World and Update Game Project.
6. Activate the event in-game and check that the Quest Journal updates.

A Quest State or QUEST DONE node can also be used as a condition for other logic. You do not need an extra trigger merely to read whether a quest has already been completed.
guides.example: Example: “Ring the bell” objective ← Bell switch ON ACTIVATE. The Journal marks that objective complete.

guides.title: 06 - Organise Visual Nodes into groups
guides.summary: Organise a large Visual Nodes graph into collapsible groups.
guides.notes:
1. Open Visual Nodes and select two or more cards that belong together.
2. Press Ctrl+G, or choose Group Selected Nodes.
3. Rename the group so its purpose is clear, for example “Castle Door Puzzle”.
4. Drag the group header to move the expanded group with its contents.
5. Collapse the group to hide its internal cards while keeping external connections visible.
6. Expand it again whenever you need to edit its contents. Save Graph + World to keep the layout.

Collapsing a group does not disable its game logic. Ungroup separates the original cards again. Group names and positions are for organisation only.
guides.example: Example: Group the two switch nodes, AND condition and door action as “Entrance Puzzle”.

guides.title: 07 - Move, zoom and save a Visual Nodes graph
guides.summary: Move around the Visual Nodes canvas and save your changes safely.
guides.notes:
1. Open Visual Nodes and use the mouse wheel or zoom controls to inspect the graph.
2. Hold the middle mouse button and drag to pan around large graphs.
3. Move cards and groups to make the connections easier to follow.
4. Use Undo/Redo if you move or edit something by mistake.
5. Choose Save Graph + World when you have changed connections, actions or the layout.

The editor saves both game behaviour and the visual arrangement. Moving a card does not change what the player experiences, but changing a connection can. When another editor has modified the graph or world, reload before overwriting its newer changes.
guides.example: Try it: Move your switch and door nodes closer together, group them, then save and reopen the graph.

guides.title: 01 - Travel between different worlds
guides.summary: Build a game with more than one world and travel between them.
guides.notes:
A World is a separate level or area with its own map and placed objects. A game can contain several worlds, such as a village and a forest.

1. Open World Manager and create another world.
2. Design each world's map and place its Player Start.
3. Configure a doorway or transition in the first world to lead to the second.
4. Select the destination world and the intended start position.
5. Create a return route if players should be able to travel back.
6. Save, Update Game Project and test both directions.

The game manages changing the active map and world objects. Items, quests and saved object states can persist as players travel between areas.
guides.example: Example: Village door → Forest entrance. Forest exit → Village return point.

guides.title: 02 - Choose where the player appears
guides.summary: Choose exactly where the player appears when entering a world.
guides.notes:
Each world has a default Player Start. You can also create named starts for different entrances.

1. Open the destination world in Game Designer.
2. Place or configure a Player Start where the player should appear.
3. Give it a clear name, such as “Forest West Entrance”.
4. Return to the doorway in the source world.
5. Choose the destination world and that named Player Start.
6. Save and test the doorway in-game.

Tip: Different doors can enter the same world at different locations. Be sure the arrival point is not inside a wall or hazard.
guides.example: Example: Coming from Village uses “Forest South Gate”; returning from Cave uses “Forest Cave Exit”.

guides.title: 03 - Save and load the game
guides.summary: Save progress in a slot and restore it after leaving the game.
guides.notes:
Save Points and save slots let players keep progress such as the current world, collected items, quests and switch states.

1. Configure a Save Point where the player can use it.
2. Start a new game and activate a few switches or collect an item.
3. Use the Save Point and choose an available save slot.
4. Leave the game or restart SIDBOX.
5. Choose Load Game from the title screen and select the saved slot.
6. Check that the player returns to the correct world with the previous progress.

Starting New Game begins a fresh run; it does not mean loading an earlier saved run. Test saving after moving between worlds, not only in the starting room.
guides.example: Try it: Open a door and collect a gem → Save → restart → Load → check both are still as saved.

guides.title: 04 - Title screens, death and world transitions
guides.summary: Add a title screen, handle player death and make world transitions smoother.
guides.notes:
1. Open the game's Title Screen settings in Game Designer.
2. Enable the title screen and choose text or PPB artwork for its appearance.
3. Optionally choose background music.
4. Configure New Game and Load Game options as needed.
5. Choose a transition effect, such as Fade or Circle, for entering or leaving worlds.
6. Save Design, Update Game Project and test beginning, loading and dying in the game.

New Game resets the current adventure. Load Game restores a saved slot. If the player dies without a usable save, the game can return to the title screen. A death message can explain what happened.
guides.example: Try it: Create a title image, select Fade for transitions, then test New Game and Load Game separately.

guides.title: 05 - Create a World Map and Quest Journal
guides.summary: Create an overview World Map and customise the Quest Journal.
guides.notes:
A World Map is an overview screen showing important locations. It is separate from the detailed ground tiles used during gameplay.

1. Open World Map Designer.
2. Choose a registered Tile Atlas and palette for the map artwork.
3. Paint the overview and place markers for your worlds.
4. Save the map and open it in the running game to check readability.
5. Open Quest Journal Designer to change its appearance, including palette, icons and layout.

The Inventory and Quest Journal screens pause ordinary gameplay while the player reads them. The World Map's artwork does not change the collision or tile graphics inside your individual worlds.
guides.example: Example: Paint a simple island overview with markers for Village, Forest and Cave.

guides.title: 06 - Add weather, day/night and particles
guides.summary: Give each world atmosphere with weather, time of day and particles.
guides.notes:
1. Open a world's settings in Game Designer.
2. Choose a weather effect, such as rain or snow, and adjust its available options.
3. Set up the day/night clock or colour changes if you want lighting to change over time.
4. To add scenery particles, place a sprite and configure it as a Particle Spawner.
5. Choose a suitable effect, such as leaves, dust or fireflies, and use the live preview.
6. Choose whether particles appear behind or in front of the player, then save and test the scene.

Weather and particles add atmosphere; they do not automatically make a floor slippery or damage the player. Those effects need separately configured collision or game logic.
guides.example: Try it: Give a forest gentle rain, a darkening evening sky and fireflies behind the player.

guides.title: 07 - Make a HUD for Health and other player stats
guides.summary: Show Health and other player values on a HUD and reuse player profiles.
guides.notes:
A HUD (heads-up display) shows information during gameplay, such as Health, points or a custom Fear meter.

1. Open the Player or Player Profile settings and choose the values to track.
2. Open HUD Editor and add a number, bar or other indicator.
3. Bind that indicator to the correct stat, such as Player Health or Fear.
4. Choose its position or dock it along an edge of the game screen.
5. Add a pickup or hazard that changes the stat.
6. Save, Update Game Project and watch the indicator during play.

Player and Physics Profiles let several worlds reuse movement and control settings. A world can select its starting profile, while game actions may change it later.
guides.example: Try it: Add a Health bar, then create a Health pickup that visibly increases it.

guides.title: 01 - Choose enemy drops and rewards
guides.summary: Choose what an enemy drops when defeated: a unique reward or repeatable loot.
guides.notes:
1. Place a sprite and configure it as Stompable Enemy.
2. Set how many hits it needs before defeat.
3. For an important one-time reward, create a hidden Collectable and choose it as the enemy's Unique drop.
4. For common drops, use Random loot pool and select eligible repeatable items such as Coins, Health or Gems.
5. A non-quest Custom Collectable must explicitly allow repeatable enemy loot before it can join the random pool.
6. Save the design and defeat a few enemies to test the results.

A unique quest reward cannot be assigned to several enemies or added to a repeatable random pool. Key and quest items are not random repeatable loot. The editor warns when selected options contradict each other.
guides.example:
Example: Boss → Unique drop: Ancient Key.
Ordinary slime → Random loot: Coin or Health.

guides.title: 02 - Add optional melee attacks
guides.summary: Add an optional close-range player attack and enemy hit feedback.
guides.notes:
1. Open Player Profile settings.
2. Enable the optional Melee attack if the game should have combat.
3. Choose the available attack reach and animation settings.
4. Configure a Stompable Enemy with a suitable hit count.
5. Enable or adjust its hit feedback where available.
6. Save Design, Update Game Project and test attacking the enemy.

Melee is optional. You can leave it disabled in games focused on exploring, talking to characters or solving puzzles. Enemies can also respond to configured player collision and other game events.
guides.example: Try it: Set an enemy to survive three hits and watch its hit feedback before the final blow.

guides.title: 03 - Flood Fill: paint or erase a whole area
guides.summary: Fill or erase a connected part of the tilemap in one action.
guides.notes:
Flood Fill is the paint bucket in the Tilemap Editor. It changes an entire connected area of matching tiles.

1. Open Tilemap Editor and choose a normal Tile Atlas graphic.
2. Click the bucket in Paint Graphics, or press F.
3. Left-click the map to fill a connected region with the selected graphic.
4. Right-click to erase a connected region.
5. Press Ctrl+Z to undo the whole fill or Ctrl+Y to redo it.
6. Press F again when you want to paint individual tiles.

Fill travels horizontally and vertically through matching cells, not diagonally. Collision Stamp placements are protected. If you want to change collision only, choose Don't change graphic and a collision brush.
guides.example: Try it: Paint the outline of a pond, select a water tile, then fill the inside with one click.

guides.title: 04 - Keep the built game smaller automatically
guides.summary: Understand how Game Builder keeps embedded map and image files smaller.
guides.notes:
Games have a limited amount of storage space. When a map contains many repeated values, CoderGirl can automatically compress those values in an embedded game build.

1. Choose Embedded map export when you want the tilemap included in the game.
2. Save Design and Update Game Project as usual.
3. Build and look at the final application size.
4. Compare results after making larger or more detailed levels.

This is automatic; you do not need to enable a special compression switch or edit generated files. Files stored separately on the TF/SD card are still separate files. A compressed map uses memory again when it is loaded, so a smaller built application does not automatically mean lower gameplay RAM use.
guides.example: Example: A map with many repeated empty or ground tiles usually compresses better than one filled with random tile numbers.

guides.title: 05 - Fix game errors before exporting
guides.summary: Fix missing resources and broken links before exporting a game.
guides.notes:
Update Game Project runs a publishing check (preflight) before generating the game files.

1. Save Design and choose Update Game Project.
2. If a problem list appears, read the first error.
3. Click Go to Problem to open the relevant editor or item.
4. Fix the missing graphic, incorrect target or invalid connection.
5. If a safe Auto Fix option is offered, check what it will change before accepting it.
6. Repeat Update Game Project until blocking errors are gone.

Errors must be fixed before export continues. Warnings explain things worth checking and may allow you to continue. A valid inventory icon can come from either a Sprite PPB or a Tile Atlas PPB.
guides.example: Example: A door targets a deleted switch → Go to Problem → choose an existing target → retry Update Game Project.

guides.title: 06 - Build the game and check its size
guides.summary: Build a V1 game and read the progress and size information.
guides.notes:
1. Save Design and choose Update Game Project.
2. Open Project Settings → Compiler.
3. Choose how many compiler jobs to use. Four is the usual starting choice; you can use 1–8 depending on your computer.
4. Choose the size-oriented -Os optimisation if appropriate for your project.
5. Click Build and watch the progress indicator.
6. After building, review Total, RAM, APP and Budget to check whether the game fits your target.

APP and Budget describe built-file size, while RAM reports known static allocations. They do not tell you the highest memory use during gameplay. Large maps, many effects or loaded images may still need runtime testing on real hardware.
guides.example: Beginner build routine: Update Game Project → Build → check for errors → check Budget → run on SIDBOX.
